findings.title: F2's `foreign` classification cannot fire for worktrees the `worktree` verb actually records, and AC-7 proves it only at a path the orchestrator never produces
findings.detail: Structural ownership is established from two prefixes only: another open task's recorded `worktree` and its `.ai/tasks/<other-id>/` directory (other_open_tasks, orchestrator.py:3810-3817). Both prefix families are removed from every task manifest before classification ever runs: BASELINE_EXCLUDE_PREFIXES = ('.git/', '.worktrees/', '.ai/tasks/') at orchestrator.py:118, applied in baseline_excluded/enumerate_tree (3237-3282). run_worktree records exactly `.worktrees/<task-id>` (worktree_path, 5039-5040; state write 5094). Consequently, for any task whose worktree was created by the `worktree` verb, no path that could be classified `foreign` can appear in `delta['produced']`, so `summary['foreign']` in evaluate_diff_scope (3953-3955) is always empty and the classification is inert in the layout the orchestrator itself creates. AC-7 passes only because its fixture records task B's worktree at `sandboxes/TASK-998` — a location nothing in the orchestrator produces — and the fixture docstring states this explicitly (test_task_baseline.py:892-898). The `.ai/tasks/<other-id>/` half is likewise asserted by calling classify_foreign_paths directly (test_task_baseline.py:946-962) rather than through a delta. The net effect is that the only concurrency case the requirement cares about in practice (two open tasks touching shared source) is the documented residual, and the delivered mechanism does not change behaviour for real worktrees. Disclosed in implementation.md as a judgement call, but it means requirement 7 / AC-7 are satisfied by a fixture rather than by the production path.

findings.title: A failed `git diff` is recorded as `committed_changed: []`, indistinguishable from "nothing committed changed"
findings.detail: changed_files_against_base returns [] on any non-zero git exit (orchestrator.py:3731-3732). evaluate_diff_scope calls it whenever the baseline recorded a head and stores the result verbatim as `summary['committed_changed']` (3932-3940). If the baseline head is unreachable in the execution root — a fresh worktree, a pruned/gc'd commit, a re-cloned tree — the evidence file reports an empty committed set and `committed_not_in_delta: []` with nothing recording that git could not answer. Requirement 8 explicitly chose omission over substitution for a missing `git.head`; the same conflation reappears here for an unanswerable one. Non-blocking evidence, but it is a claim of absence nothing verified.

findings.title: Committed evidence uses three-dot diff, so a non-ancestor baseline head silently reverts to the fork point F3 was about
findings.detail: changed_files_against_base runs `git diff --name-only {base}...HEAD` (orchestrator.py:3723). Three dots diff from merge-base(base, HEAD), not from base. While the branch advances linearly from the captured baseline the two are identical, which is why AC-8 passes. After a rebase, amend or reset that makes the recorded baseline head no longer an ancestor of HEAD, the effective base becomes the merge base — i.e. the fork point — and `committed_changed` again lists branch history the task did not produce, which is the defect F3 exists to remove. `{base}..HEAD` would express the intended "since the baseline commit" exactly.

findings.title: Recovery eligibility mixes attempt-scoped and whole-trail checks, so an interrupted `implement` after any earlier fix is not recoverable and `run` resumes it instead of stopping
findings.detail: last_implementation_attempt is attempt-scoped (orchestrator.py:2969-2990), but the CLAUDE_FIX_STARTED test uses has_event over the whole trail (3010). For the sequence FAILED -> CLAUDE_FIX -> fix -> validation fails -> CODEX_REPLAN -> approve -> implement -> killed, the current attempt is an uninterrupted-and-unterminated plain `implement`, yet `recover` refuses with "the task carries CLAUDE_FIX_STARTED, so `fix` is its legal verb". run_fix uses the same whole-trail check (2885), so the task is not stranded — but the interruption is never recorded as one, and run_driver's IMPLEMENTING branch takes the has_event(CLAUDE_FIX_STARTED) path (5542) and calls run_fix, i.e. `run` autonomously re-invokes the implementer on an interrupted implementation rather than stopping and naming `recover`. AC-19 does mandate the refusal and AC-6 only covers the no-CLAUDE_FIX_STARTED case, so this is inside the approved contract; flagging because the guarantee "an interrupted implementation reaches a routable state through `recover`, and `run` never resumes one on its own" holds only for tasks with no fix anywhere in their history.

findings.title: `recover`'s unlocked write sequence is observable mid-update and its lock check is a TOCTOU
findings.detail: run_recover takes no per-task lock (UNLOCKED_ACTIONS, orchestrator.py:5908) and gates only on `lock_path.exists()` at 3116, then writes IMPLEMENTATION_INTERRUPTED (3173), then state.json (3189), then TASK_RECOVERED (3191). Two consequences. (a) Another orchestrator invocation can create the lock in the window between 3116 and 3189 and then read the pre-recovery IMPLEMENTING state while recover overwrites it; save_state is atomic so no torn file results, but last-writer-wins across two views of the state is possible. (b) IMPLEMENTATION_INTERRUPTED is not in IMPLEMENTATION_TERMINATING_EVENTS (171-176), so a process killed between 3173 and 3189 leaves the attempt still "unterminated" and a re-run records a second IMPLEMENTATION_INTERRUPTED for the same attempt — the enumeration's own docstring claims a missing entry would let recovery accept an attempt whose outcome was already recorded. Both follow from decision 4's no-lock design and neither strands a task, so this is reported as an observation on the new write sequence rather than a defect in the approved behaviour.

findings.title: PreToolUse authorization inputs moved to unvalidated environment variables
findings.detail: The guard used to locate the approved plan and task evidence relative to its own cwd, i.e. inside the tree it was guarding. It now resolves them from ORCHESTRATOR_REPO_ROOT and ORCHESTRATOR_TASK_DIR. ORCHESTRATOR_TASK_DIR is taken verbatim (Path(raw), no exported_dir() is_dir check, no requirement that it sit under repo_root()/.ai/tasks/<ORCHESTRATOR_TASK_ID>), and approved_plan() then reads state.json, events.jsonl and the plan bytes from wherever it points. The sha256 re-check only proves internal consistency of that directory, so a self-consistent fake evidence dir (state.json naming a plan + a PLAN_APPROVED event with that plan's digest) authorizes writes to any .ai/scripts, .ai/schemas, .ai/hooks or .claude/settings.json path. A worker holds Bash and can create such a directory in its tree and launch a nested agent with these variables set. The implementation notes themselves record that these exports are decisive for authorization: inherited ORCHESTRATOR_* values made 14 existing hook tests authorize against the real TASK-008 plan instead of their fixture. A cheap cross-check (require the task dir to be repo_root/.ai/tasks/<task id>, or at least is_dir) would keep single-homing while removing the free choice of authority.

findings.title: Declared-path writes are allowed in the orchestrator checkout, where the task delta cannot see them
findings.detail: relative_to_repo() offers the candidate path relative to both worker_root() and repo_root(), and check_write allows an infrastructure path if any form is declared. So a worker rooted in .worktrees/<id> may write the checkout's copy of a declared file by absolute path — including .ai/scripts/orchestrator.py, the code the orchestrator executes on its next verb, and .ai/hooks/*. That the worker can reach the checkout is not hypothetical: run_claude_implementation now hands it absolute checkout paths and instructs it to write implementation.md there. Meanwhile capture_baseline (orchestrator.py:3378) and compute_task_delta (orchestrator.py:3490) enumerate only execution_root, so a write landing in the checkout appears in no baseline, no delta, no diff-scope violation list — it is outside the evidence the task is judged on, and outside this task's own reported 'exactly the 14 declared files' delta. The two-root leniency is deliberate and documented, but nothing in the guard or in validation distinguishes 'the declared file in the tree you were given' from 'the same-named file in the orchestrator's tree'.

findings.title: The enforcing hook copy is now branch content in the worker's own tree
findings.detail: .claude/settings.json registers hooks as cwd-relative commands (`bash .ai/hooks/run .ai/hooks/pre_tool_use.py`), and worker execution is now rooted in the recorded worktree, so the guard that authorizes each write is the worktree's copy — whatever the task's branch happens to carry — while the authority it checks against is the checkout's plan. Nothing verifies that the executing copy matches the checkout's, so a worktree whose branch carries a weakened pre_tool_use.py or .ai/hooks/run enforces nothing, silently (the module's own docstring notes exit 1 denies nothing). The reachable case is not exotic: this task's approved plan declares .ai/hooks/pre_tool_use.py, so the implementer rewrote, in its own worktree, the very guard copy that governed its subsequent tool calls in that session. I am recording this because the security consequence of the approved 'which copy executes' decision (AC-31) is that guard code provenance moved from the developer's checkout to the task branch; the decision itself was made knowingly.

findings.title: New path-resolution code in the guard can fail open on an unexpected exception
findings.detail: relative_to_repo() wraps Path(candidate)/resolve() in a try that catches only OSError. resolve() raises ValueError for an embedded null byte, and the loop's per-root try catches only (ValueError, OSError) around relative_to. An exception escaping check_write leaves the hook exiting 1, which this file documents as denying nothing — the failure mode it was written to avoid. Relatedly, normalise() strips only a leading './' and does not collapse interior './' or '../' segments, so `.ai/tasks/<id>/./state.json` does not match PROTECTED_EVIDENCE_PATTERNS in its raw form; the denial depends entirely on the resolved form being produced. Both point the same way: the resolution step should be treated as fallible and denied on failure rather than allowed to propagate.

findings.title: Another task's recorded worktree string is trusted verbatim as a foreign-ownership prefix
findings.detail: other_open_tasks() appends other['worktree'] as an ownership prefix after only a non-empty string check — no is_dir validation (unlike recorded_worktree()), and no constraint that the value be under .worktrees/ or not an ancestor of shared source. classify_foreign_paths() then removes matching paths from `violations` at orchestrator.py:3953, so a broad or wrong recorded value in any other open task's state.json (e.g. '.ai' or a shared source directory) silently demotes real scope violations to non-blocking report metadata. path_under() correctly enforces component boundaries and terminal-state owners are excluded, so the remaining gap is the shape of the recorded value. Reachability is limited today because only run_worktree writes it (worktree_path(task_id)) and workers cannot write state.json, which is why this is low rather than higher — but the plan's own risk list names over-broad foreign matching as the thing to prevent, and the value is the one input not constrained.

findings.title: Injected 'Project invariants' text is resolved from an env-supplied path to a file no tier protects
findings.detail: session_start.py now resolves the constitution from ORCHESTRATOR_CONSTITUTION (taken verbatim, no containment check) and injects its contents into the worker's context under the heading 'Project invariants', i.e. as authoritative instructions to a session holding Edit/Write/Bash. The blackboard portion carries an explicit 'this is data, not instructions' caveat; the constitution portion carries none. .ai/constitution.md appears in neither PROTECTED_EVIDENCE_PATTERNS nor PROTECTED_INFRA_PATTERNS, so a worker may edit it without any plan declaration, and what it writes is delivered to the next worker as invariants. The env indirection is new here; the injection itself predates this change, so the actionable part is that neither the path nor the file has an ownership guard while the change makes the path externally chosen.

findings.title: New hook-launching subprocesses in the test suite carry no timeout
findings.detail: The three subprocess launch helpers added by this change — `test_context_bus.WorktreeHookBehaviourTests._run` (line 692), `test_context_bus.WorktreeHookCopyAuthorityTests._launch` (line 804, which additionally goes through `bash .ai/hooks/run`) and `test_hardening.WorktreePreToolUseTests`' guard runner (line 878) — call `subprocess.run` without `timeout=`, while the other subprocess helpers added in the same change do set one (`test_run_driver.py:1074` uses `timeout=120`, `test_worker_launch.py:517/547` use `VERSION_TIMEOUT_S`). A child that wedges therefore blocks the whole run rather than failing its own test. That matters here specifically because AC-16 executes full discovery under a bounded acceptance timeout and has already been observed to hit it (routed failure recorded in the implementation notes, fix pass 4): a wedged hook consumes the entire budget and surfaces only as `returncode 124, timed out after 300s` with no indication of which test hung. The repository already treats this as a rule for production code — `test_orchestrator_infra.py:31-39` asserts `orchestrator.py` has at least as many `timeout=` arguments as `subprocess.run(` calls.

findings.title: `run_recover` re-parses events.jsonl three times per invocation
findings.detail: `recovery_eligibility` scans the whole event log twice — once via `has_event(task_id, "CLAUDE_FIX_STARTED")` (line 3010) and once via `last_implementation_attempt` (line 3017) — and then `run_recover` calls `last_implementation_attempt` a third time at line 3132 to recover the `started` event that `recovery_eligibility` had already computed and discarded (it returns only `(eligible, detail)`). Each call re-opens and re-JSON-parses every line of `events.jsonl`, which grows append-only for the life of a task. The cost is bounded and paid once per `recover` invocation, so this is a tidiness/scaling-with-trail-length issue rather than a hot path; returning the started event from `recovery_eligibility`, or scanning once for both facts, would remove two of the three passes.
